﴿He frowned and turned away, because the blind man came to him. And what would make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself, or be reminded, and the reminder would benefit him.﴾

In this passage there are six issues.

The first concerns His saying, exalted is He: ʿabasa (he frowned), meaning he contracted his face. It is said: ʿabasa wa basara. This has already been discussed. Tawalla (he turned away) means he turned his face away. Anna jāʾahu (because he came to him): anna is in the accusative position because it is a mafʿūl lahu (object of purpose, an accusative noun giving the reason for the action). The meaning is "because the blind man came to him," that is, the one who cannot see with his eyes.

The commentators unanimously related that a group of the notables of Quraysh were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he had hoped for their Islam. Then ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm came, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked that ʿAbdullāh should interrupt his speech, so he turned away from him, and this verse was revealed concerning that.

Mālik said: Hishām ibn ʿUrwa narrated to him from ʿUrwa that he said: "ʿAbasa wa tawallā was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktūm. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and began saying: 'O Muhammad, bring me near (istadnini)...'" [[The narration here and in Ibn al-ʿArabī reads "O Muhammad," while the well-known version in the books of tafsir is "O Messenger of Allah, teach me of what Allah has taught you." In another narration: "O Messenger of Allah, guide me," as the author will mention later.]] And with the Prophet (ﷺ) was a man from the great polytheists, so the Prophet (ﷺ) kept turning away from him and turning toward the other, saying: "O so-and-so, do you see any harm in what I say?" He would say: "No, by the idols (al-dumā), I see no harm in what you say." [[al-Dumā: plural of dumya, meaning an image; he means the idols.]] [[What is between the brackets is missing from manuscript B.]] So Allah revealed: ﴿He frowned and turned away.﴾

In al-Tirmidhī, with a chain of narration, he said: Saʿīd ibn Yahyā ibn Saʿīd al-Umawī narrated to us, my father narrated to me, and he said: "This is what we presented to Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from his father, from ʿĀʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: ʿAbasa wa tawallā was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktūm, the blind man. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and began saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, guide me.' With the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was a man from the great polytheists, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) kept turning away from him and turning toward the other, saying: 'Do you see any harm in what I say?' He would say: 'No.' So this was revealed." He said: This is a gharīb (rare) hadith.

The second issue: the verse is a rebuke from Allah to His Prophet (ﷺ) for his turning away and his frowning at ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm. It is also said: ʿAmr ibn Umm Maktūm. The name of Umm Maktūm was ʿĀtika bint ʿĀmir ibn Makhzūm. This ʿAmr is the son of Qays ibn Zāʾida ibn al-Aṣamm, and he was the nephew (son of the maternal uncle) of Khadīja (may Allah be pleased with her). He had been occupied with a man from the great polytheists, who is said to have been al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra. Ibn al-ʿArabī (a classical jurist and Qur'an scholar, Ibn al-ʿArabī al-Mālikī) said: "This was said by the Mālikī scholars among our scholars, and he was called Abū ʿAbd Shams." Qatāda said: it was Umayya ibn Khalaf, and from him (another report): Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Mujāhid said: they were three: ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabīʿa, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf. ʿAṭāʾ said: ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa. Sufyān al-Thawrī said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was with his uncle al-ʿAbbās. al-Zamakhsharī said: with him were the chieftains of Quraysh: ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabīʿa, Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, whom he was calling to Islam, hoping that others would become Muslim through their Islam.

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: As for the saying of our scholars that it was al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, others have said it was Umayya ibn Khalaf and al-ʿAbbās. All of this is false and ignorance on the part of the commentators who did not verify the religion. That is because Umayya ibn Khalaf and al-Walīd were in Mecca, while Ibn Umm Maktūm was in Medina; he was never present with them, nor were they present with him. Both of them died as disbelievers: one before the Hijra, and the other at Badr. Umayya never intended Medina, nor was he ever present with him, alone or with anyone.

The third issue: Ibn Umm Maktūm came while the Prophet (ﷺ) was occupied with those of the notables of Quraysh who were present, calling them to Allah, the Exalted. His hope for their Islam had grown strong, and in their Islam was the Islam of those behind them from their people. Ibn Umm Maktūm, who was blind, came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, teach me of what Allah has taught you." He kept calling out and repeating his call, not realizing that the Prophet (ﷺ) was occupied with someone else, until the displeasure appeared on the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) because he had interrupted his speech. He (the Prophet) said to himself: "These people will say: his followers are only the blind, the lowly, and the slaves." So he frowned and turned away from him, and the verse was revealed.

al-Thawrī said: After that, whenever the Prophet (ﷺ) saw Ibn Umm Maktūm, he would spread out his cloak for him and say: "Welcome to the one for whom my Lord rebuked me." He would also say: "Do you need anything?" He appointed him as his deputy over Medina twice, during two expeditions he undertook. Anas said: "I saw him on the day of al-Qādisiyya, riding, wearing armor, and with him a black banner."

The fourth issue: Our scholars said: what Ibn Umm Maktūm did was a lack of proper manners, had he known that the Prophet (ﷺ) was occupied with others and that he hoped for their Islam. But Allah, blessed and exalted, rebuked him, so that the hearts of the People of the Ṣuffa would not be broken, or to make known that a believing poor man is better than a rich one. Looking to the believer, even if he is poor, is more fitting and more appropriate than the other matter, which is turning toward the rich in hope of their faith, even though that too is a kind of benefit. On this basis is understood His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for a prophet to have captives until he has inflicted slaughter (in the land)﴾ [al-Anfāl: 67], and the rest of the verse, according to what has already been mentioned. [[See vol. 8, p. 45 and following.]]

It is also said: the Prophet (ﷺ) only intended to win over that man, trusting in the faith that was in the heart of Ibn Umm Maktūm, as he said: "I join ties with a man while another is dearer to me than him, out of fear that Allah would cast him on his face into the Fire." [[The sense of this report is ascribed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the sources, though its wording varies.]]

The fifth issue: Ibn Zayd said: The Prophet (ﷺ) only frowned at Ibn Umm Maktūm and turned away from him because he gestured to the one who was leading him to hold him back, so Ibn Umm Maktūm pushed him away, and insisted on speaking to the Prophet (ﷺ) until he taught him. So there was in this a kind of rudeness on his part. Despite this, Allah revealed concerning him to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, using the form of speaking about an absent person, out of honoring him [[In manuscripts A and H: "taʿlīman" (teaching) instead of "taʿẓīman" (honoring).]], and did not say: "You frowned and turned away." Then He turned to him directly, addressing him to put him at ease, and said: ﴿And what would make you know?﴾, that is, what would inform you? ﴿Perhaps he would purify himself﴾, meaning Ibn Umm Maktūm, by what he asked of you, namely your teaching him the Qur'an and the religion, so that he would grow in purity in his religion and the darkness of ignorance would be removed from him.

It is also said: the pronoun in ﴿perhaps he﴾ refers to the disbeliever. That is, if you hope that he would purify himself through Islam, or ﴿be reminded, so the reminder would bring him closer to accepting the truth﴾. And what would make you know that what you hoped for will come to pass?

al-Ḥasan recited: ﴿Aʾan jāʾahu al-aʿmā﴾ [[al-Zamakhsharī said: it was recited as (aʾan) with two hamzas and an alif between them.]] with a madd (lengthening) as an interrogative, so anna is connected to a verb that is omitted, indicated by ʿabasa wa tawallā. The sense is: "Did he frown and turn away because the blind man came to him?" According to this reading one stops at tawallā, and one does not stop on it according to the recitation of the rest of the readers, which is the common recitation.

The sixth issue: a similar verse of rebuke is His saying, exalted is He, in Sūrat al-Anʿām: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-Anʿām: 52]. Likewise His saying in Sūrat al-Kahf: ﴿And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and what is similar to it. And Allah knows best.

﴿Or be reminded﴾, meaning he takes admonition from what you say, ﴿so the reminder would benefit him﴾, that is, the admonition.

The common recitation is (fa-tanfaʿuhu) with a ḍamma on the ʿayn, as a conjunction after yazzakkā. ʿĀṣim, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and ʿĪsā recited fa-tanfaʿahu with a fatḥa (accusative), and this is the recitation of al-Sulamī and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh. It is in the accusative as an answer after laʿalla (perhaps), because it is not an affirmative statement, like His saying: ﴿Perhaps I may reach the means﴾ [Ghāfir: 36], then ﴿so that I may look up﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 55].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 80, verses 11–16:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay, indeed it is a reminder﴾. *Kalla* (nay) is a word of refusal and rebuke, meaning: the matter is not as you are doing with the two groups; that is, do not do the like of it again, namely, turning your attention to the wealthy man and turning away from the poor believer. What occurred from the Prophet (ﷺ) was leaving what is better (*tark al-awla*), as has already been mentioned. **Qurtubi's commentary on Surah ʿAbasa (80:17–23)**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Destroyed is man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ "Qutila" means "cursed" (lu'ina). It was also said that it means "tortured" (ʿudhdhiba). "Al-insan" here means the disbelieving man.

Al-Aʿmash related from Mujahid that he said: "Wherever in the Qur'an 'qutila al-insan' occurs, it refers to the disbeliever."

Al-Dahhak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "It was revealed concerning ʿUtba ibn Abi Lahab. He had believed, but when Surat al-Najm (the Star) was revealed, he apostatised and said: 'I believed in the whole Qur'an except al-Najm.' So Allah, Majestic is His praise, revealed concerning him: 'Qutila al-insan,' meaning: cursed is ʿUtba, since he disbelieved in the Qur'an. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invoked against him and said: [O Allah, set against him Your dog, the lion of al-Ghadira].[[As the wording of the hadith stands in the sources; but in Abu Hayyan's narration it is: 'O Allah, send upon him Your dog to devour him.' Then he said: 'When he reached al-Ghadira...' etc.]] So he set out at once with merchandise for Syria. When he reached al-Ghadira, he remembered the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ), so he offered those with him a thousand dinars if he woke up alive. They placed him in the middle of the caravan and put the goods all around him. While they were in that state, a lion approached. When it came near the baggage, it leapt, and there it was upon him, tearing him apart. His father had mourned him and wept, saying: 'Muhammad has never said anything at all but that it came to pass.'"

Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿how ungrateful he is!﴾ that it means: "What is it that makes him so ungrateful?" It was also said that it is an expression of wonder. It is the custom of the Arabs, when they marvel at something, to say: "May Allah fight him, how fine he is!" or "May Allah humiliate him, how unjust he is!" The meaning is: marvel at the disbelief of man in respect of all that we have mentioned after this.

It was also said: "How ungrateful he is towards Allah and His blessings, despite knowing the abundance of His kindness to him," also as an expression of wonder. Ibn Jurayj said: "That is, how severe his disbelief is!"

It was also said that "ma" is interrogative, meaning: "What has led him to disbelief?" This is then a question of rebuke. "Ma" may carry the sense of wonder, and it may carry the sense of "ayy" (which), in which case it is interrogative.

﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾ That is: from what thing did Allah create this disbeliever, so that he should be proud? I.e., marvel at his creation. ﴿From a drop of seminal fluid﴾: that is, from a small, despicable, lifeless water. He created him, yet he did not go astray in himself?! Al-Hasan said: "How can one who came out through the passage of urine twice be proud?" ﴿Then He measured him﴾ in his mother's womb. Thus al-Dahhak related from Ibn ʿAbbas: that is, He measured his hands, feet, eyes, and all his other limbs, and (his being) handsome or ugly, short or tall, wretched or happy.

It was also said: "fa-qaddarahu" means "fa-sawwahu" (He fashioned him), as He said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop, then fashioned you as a man?﴾ and He said: ﴿Who created you and fashioned you?﴾

It was also said: "fa-qaddarahu atwaran" means: from one state to another: a drop, then a clinging clot, until his creation was complete.

﴿Then He made the way easy for him﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, in the transmission of ʿAta', Qatada, al-Suddi, and Muqatil, said: He made it easy for him to come out of his mother's womb. Mujahid said: He made it easy for him (to know) the path of good and evil, that is, He clarified that for him. Its proof is: ﴿Indeed We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful﴾ and ﴿We guided him to the two highways﴾. This was also said by al-Hasan, ʿAta', and Ibn ʿAbbas, in the transmission of Abu Salih from him. And from Mujahid also: "The way of wretchedness and happiness." Ibn Zayd said: "The way of Islam." Abu Bakr ibn Tahir said: He made easy for every person that for which He created him and decreed it upon him. Its proof is the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him): [Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created].

﴿Then He made him die and gave him a grave﴾: that is, He made for him a grave in which he is concealed, as an honour, and did not make him one of those cast upon the face of the earth, to be eaten by birds and beasts (al-ʿawafi).[[Al-ʿawafi: those who seek sustenance among people, animals and birds; the intended meaning here is wild beasts and cattle.]] This was said by al-Farra'. Abu ʿUbayda said: "fa-aqbarahu" means: He made for him a grave, and commanded that he be buried. Abu ʿUbayda said: When ʿUmar ibn Hubayra killed Salih ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, the Banu Tamim said, entering upon him: "Give us Salih for burial." He said: "Take him." He said: "fa-aqbarahu" and did not say "qabarahu," because the one who buries (qabir) is the one who buries with his own hand. Al-Aʿsha said:

*If she had leaned a dead man against her neck, he would have lived, and not been carried to the one who buries.*

One says: "qabartu al-mayyit" when I bury the dead; and "aqbarahu Allah" means: He made him into one who is buried, and made for him a grave. The Arabs say: "batartu dhanab al-baʿir" (I cut off the camel's tail), and "abtarahu Allah"; and "ʿadabtu qarn al-thawr" (I broke the bull's horn), and "aʿdabahu Allah"; and "tartu fulanan" (I drove away so-and-so), and "Allah aṭradahu," meaning: He made him one who is driven away.

﴿Then, when He wills, He will raise him up﴾: that is, He will bring him back to life after his death. The common reading is "anshharahu" with an alif. Abu Haywa related from Nafiʿ and Shuʿayb ibn Abi Hamza "shaʾa nashharahu" without alif. They are two eloquent dialects with the same meaning. It is said: "Anshara Allah al-mayyit" and "nashara-hu" (Allah raised the dead). Al-Aʿsha said:

*Until people say, of what they saw: "How strange, for the dead one who rises!"*

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but he has not fulfilled what He commanded him﴾. Mujahid and Qatada said: "Lamma yaqdi" means: no one fulfils what he was commanded. Ibn ʿAbbas used to say: "Lamma yaqdi ma amarahu" means: he did not fulfil the covenant that was taken from him in the loins of Adam. Then it was said: "Kalla" is a rebuke and a warning, meaning: the matter is not as the disbeliever says. For when the disbeliever is told of the resurrection, he says: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, surely I shall have the best with Him﴾, and perhaps says: "I have fulfilled what I was commanded." So He said: "Nay, he has fulfilled nothing; rather, he disbelieves in Me and in My Messenger." Al-Hasan said: "That is, truly, he has not fulfilled: that is, he has not acted upon what he was commanded." The "lamma" in His saying "lamma" is an expletive particle of speech, like His saying: ﴿By a mercy from Allah﴾ and His saying: ﴿After a little, they will surely become regretful﴾.

Imam Ibn Fawrak said: That is: "Kalla, lamma yaqdi Allah li-hadha al-kafir ma amarahu bihi min al-iman," meaning: Allah has not decreed for this disbeliever what He commanded him of faith; rather, He commanded him with what He had not decreed for him. Ibn al-Anbari said: Stopping at "kalla" is ugly, while stopping at "amarahu" and "anshharahu" is good; in that case "kalla" means "truly" (haqqan).

It is the second blast of the Trumpet, which deafens the ears: that is, it deafens them, so that they hear only what is called out to the living.

Some of the exegetes mentioned that they said: the ears will be attentive to it (tuṣīḵhu), from your saying "aṣākha ilā kadhā", meaning he listened to it. From this is the hadith: "There is no creature except that it is attentive on the day of Friday, out of fear of the Hour, except the jinn and mankind." The poet said:

It turns its ears toward the faint sound,
Attentive as a listener to a reciter.

Some scholars said: this is taken as an acceptance of the earlier authorities. As for the language, its implication is the first opinion. Al-Khalil said: al-Sakhkhah is a cry that deafens the ears (ṣakhkhan), that is, it deafens them with the severity of its impact. The original meaning of the word in the language is a strong striking. It was also said that it is derived from "ṣakhkhahu bil-ḥajar", when he struck it with a stone. The rajaz poet said:

O my neighbor, will you contend with me
With a force like the striking of stones against boulders?

From this same usage is the Arabs' saying: "Ṣakhkhat-humu al-ṣākhkhah and bāttat-humu al-bā'itah", meaning the calamity. Al-Ṭabarī said: I think it is from "ṣakhkha fulān fulānan", when he deafened him. Ibn al-'Arabi [[We did not find this statement of Ibn al-'Arabi in the printed edition published by Maṭba'at al-Sa'ada of his book (Aḥkām al-Qur'ān).]] said: al-Sakhkhah is that which causes deafness, and indeed it is a making-to-hear, and this is from the wondrous eloquence, to the extent that one of the young poets of his time said:

The announcer deafened you, though he was hearing.

Another said:

Their secret deafened me in the days of their separation,
So have you heard of a secret that causes deafness?

By Allah's life, the Cry of the Resurrection is indeed a making-to-hear, which deafens to the world and makes the affairs of the Hereafter heard.

So the Deafening Blast comes on this day, on which a person flees from his brother, that is, from befriending his brother and conversing with him, because he has no leisure for that, being occupied with himself, as He said after it: ﴿For every man among them, on that day, is a matter that occupies him﴾, that is, it preoccupies him from others. It was also said: he flees only out of fear of their demands upon him, because of the obligations between them. It was also said: so that they do not see what he is in of severity. It was also said: because he knows that they will not benefit him and will not avail him anything, as He said: ﴿The day when no protector will avail a protector anything﴾ [al-Dukhān: 41]. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṭāhir al-Abharī said: he flees from them because of what has become clear to him of their weakness and their lack of resources, toward the One who owns the removal of those calamities and worries from him. Had this become clear to him in this world, he would not have relied on anything except his Lord, the Exalted.

﴿And his companion﴾, that is, his wife.

﴿And his sons﴾, that is, his children. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Qābīl flees from his brother Hābīl; the Prophet (ﷺ) flees from his mother; Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) flees from his father; Nūḥ (peace be upon him) flees from his son; Lūṭ flees from his wife; and Ādam flees from the shame of his sons. Al-Ḥasan said: the first to flee on the Day of Resurrection from his father is Ibrāhīm, the first to flee from his son is Nūḥ, and the first to flee from his wife is Lūṭ. He said: they consider that this verse was revealed concerning them, and this is the flight of disavowal.
